segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Opening and early New Orleans influences on Colyer
segments.summary: Interviewer sets up the 1959 session in Hounslow; Colyer says he came to New Orleans music through records after the war, citing Kid Ory/Mutt Carey, George Lewis and Bunk Johnson.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Forming the Crane River Jazz Band; New York jazz heard at sea
segments.summary: Colyer learned trumpet in the merchant navy and formed the Crane River band c. 1948-49; he recalls hearing the Condon band in New York and first playing at Cranford.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Hostile reception and the Bunk Johnson and Armstrong debate
segments.summary: Early critics were hostile to the Bunk Johnson and George Lewis records; Colyer felt they were the authentic idiom and was never greatly impressed by Armstrong.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Other British bands: Lyttelton, Randall, George Webb
segments.summary: Humphrey Lyttelton's band was top, Freddy Randall also good; Webb's Dixielanders were influenced by Lu Watters. Colyer only listened to Webb while on leave.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Winning over London audiences and finding repertoire
segments.summary: Moving from the suburbs into central London, the band won over fans by sticking to its guns and working out unfamiliar tunes, drawing on records and the Bunk Johnson style.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Why traditional jazz is bigger in Britain than the States
segments.summary: Colyer thinks British trad is larger and healthier than in America, because Britain had lost its own folk culture and jazz filled the gap.

segments.chapter: British revival and the Crane River band
segments.title: Adapting British folk and pop tunes to jazz
segments.summary: The Crane River band played 'The Miner's Dream of Home' and 'Bobby Shafto', for which Colyer claims the break arrangement; other pop tunes were easily adapted.

segments.chapter: Going to New Orleans, 1952
segments.title: Christie Brothers Stompers and back to sea
segments.summary: After Crane River split, Colyer joined the Christie Brothers Stompers for six to eight months, then rejoined the merchant navy and took a ship trading from Mobile.

segments.chapter: Going to New Orleans, 1952
segments.title: Arriving in New Orleans and first sitting in with George Lewis
segments.summary: Colyer reached New Orleans after trips on the Mobile run, heard the Octave Crosby and Paul Barbarin bands, and sat in with George Lewis' band, feeling vindicated.

segments.chapter: Going to New Orleans, 1952
segments.title: Playing with Lewis, recording sessions, and length of stay
segments.summary: He sat in with Lewis after a couple of weeks, recorded two important sessions, and stayed a little over a month before trouble with authorities, then about another month before leaving.

segments.chapter: Defending the New Orleans style
segments.title: Defending New Orleans music as a complete style
segments.summary: Answering criticism that New Orleans music disappoints, Colyer says it is a complete style he will keep playing and improving without moving on.

segments.chapter: Defending the New Orleans style
segments.title: Commercialism and contemporaries Lyttelton and Barber
segments.summary: Colyer says no one has improved on the New Orleans pattern; he is negative about Lyttelton's swing direction and Barber's drift to arranged music.

segments.chapter: Going to New Orleans, 1952
segments.title: Crane River band personnel and a brief session with Barber
segments.summary: Colyer lists the Crane River lineup including Monty Sunshine, Sonny Morris, John R.T. Davis, Ben Marshall, his brother on washboard, and no steady drummer; Barber played only one early session.

segments.chapter: Going to New Orleans, 1952
segments.title: Most influential New Orleans musicians: Percy Humphrey and others
segments.summary: Percy Humphrey was Colyer's deepest influence; he also praises DeDe Pierce and Kid Howard, and the Eureka and George Lewis bands as the greatest things.

segments.chapter: Later band, return visits and marching band
segments.title: Return to England, Denmark, and the Barber-Sunshine band
segments.summary: After the immigration matter was sorted out, he started with Chris Barber and Monty Sunshine in 1953, rehearsed in Copenhagen, then broke away after about a year to form his present band, whose members he lists.

segments.chapter: Later band, return visits and marching band
segments.title: Brief return to New Orleans, 1958
segments.summary: Colyer returned for a couple of days last year, heard the Eureka Brass Band in a parade and Kid Thomas across the river.

segments.chapter: Later band, return visits and marching band
segments.title: His own marching band and parade trouble in Britain
segments.summary: Colyer discusses his record with a marching band modeled on the Eureka, its lack of rehearsal, and parades obstructed by large second lines, including being refused at the Soho Fair.

segments.chapter: Later band, return visits and marching band
segments.title: Other New Orleans marching bands heard
segments.summary: Apart from Eureka he liked the Young Tuxedo band and recalls no others.

segments.chapter: Present state and future of British jazz
segments.title: College tour with George Lewis and Lewis' British tour
segments.summary: Colyer toured New England colleges with Lewis, still finding him in good form, and says Lewis' British tour was generally enjoyed despite critics, though Lawrence Marrero was missed.

segments.chapter: Present state and future of British jazz
segments.title: Future of British traditional jazz and current audiences
segments.summary: The amateur and semi-professional scene is lively and improving; Colyer says audiences fluctuate but he has a staunch following in Britain and Germany. The transcript ends with ASR repetition.
